subject: Biology
title: The Double Helix
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Double Helix.

hook.text: In 1953, Watson and Crick revealed DNA's shape: a twisted ladder called the double helix.

buildup.text: The sides are sugar-phosphate backbones. The rungs are pairs of bases: A with T, C with G.

discovery.text: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photograph—Photo 51—was the key clue to the structure.

twist.text: Franklin's contribution went unrecognized for decades. She died before the Nobel was awarded.

climax.text: The helix shape lets DNA unzip easily for copying, making replication fast and accurate.

punchline.text: A twisted ladder that holds all of life's secrets.

quiz.question: Whose X-ray photograph was crucial to discovering DNA's structure?

details.summary: The double helix is DNA's iconic twisted-ladder structure, discovered by Watson and Crick in 1953 using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray crystallography data. Two sugar-phosphate backbones wind around each other with complementary base pairs forming the rungs.
details.whyItMatters: Discovering the double helix structure immediately suggested how DNA replicates and stores information. It launched modern molecular biology and remains one of the most important scientific discoveries of the twentieth century.
takeaways: Adenine pairs with thymine; guanine pairs with cytosine via hydrogen bonds
Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51 provided crucial structural evidence
The complementary base pairing mechanism explains how DNA copies itself

faq.question: How did Watson and Crick discover the double helix?
faq.answer: They built physical models of possible DNA structures, guided by Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction image Photo 51 showing helical parameters, and Erwin Chargaff's rules about base ratios. The model that satisfied all constraints was the double helix.

faq.question: Why is Rosalind Franklin's contribution controversial?
faq.answer: Franklin's X-ray data was shared with Watson without her knowledge and was critical to solving the structure. She received no credit in the Nobel Prize awarded in 1962, partly because she died in 1958 and Nobels are not given posthumously.
